newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar drifts to weaker close ahead of key CPI.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar drifts to weaker close ahead of key CPI.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar drifted to a weaker close on Monday as investors shouldered arms ahead of key inflation data for the June quarter, due out on Tuesday morning (NZT).
"It's been very, very quiet today. People are obviously focusing on the CPI due out tomorrow," said a Wellington bank chief dealer.
The Kiwi, also weighed on by a weaker Australian unit, closed at US$0.6668/75 and at 65.80 on its Trade-Weighted Index, down from 0.6683/90 and 65.94 at the open.
The all-important Monetary Conditions Index stood at 758 -- 67 points below the Reserve Bank's desired level and 17 points outside its comfort zone.
On Friday the bank reprimanded the markets for easing conditions too far, but response to the statement has been muted and conditions are now almost as loose as they were then.
While dealers felt the bank would refrain from any further action until after the CPI release, they said the bank's dilemma was likely to be further compounded by Tuesday's inflation number.
"The general feeling in the market is it will be lower than expected, so I guess we can continue to test the Reserve Bank's patience," the chief dealer said.

The Reserve Bank has forecast underlying inflation at 0.3 percent in the June quarter. Economists polled by Reuters on average forecast core inflation at 0.33 percent in the June quarter for an annual rise of 1.5 percent.
The CPI number, which includes government charges, changes in interest rates charges and one-offs, is forecast by economists to come out at 0.14 percent for the quarter and 1.13 percent for the year.
Dealers said unless the CPI number was higher than expected, the Kiwi was likely to be sold.
"There's just really not a lot of buyers in the Kiwi, there's not a lot of support at the moment," said one.
"The current account numbers (on Friday last week) set the tone and I just don't think the short-term punters really want to get involved in buying Kiwi."

If the Kiwi continued to fall following the CPI, and monetary conditions continued to ease, dealers said the Reserve Bank may well cut its cash settlement target -- the amount of cash it aims to keep in the banking system overnight.
The chief dealer said while the Kiwi would bounce significantly on such a move, it would quickly come off again.

"But (Governor) Brash has always said he's wanted a lower currency and higher interest rates, so at the end of the day them changing the cash target and the currency not really recovering but interest rates being higher may possibly be what they want anyway," he said.
The Kiwi was seen trading in a 0.6660-90 range heading into the CPI release at 10.45 a.m. on Tuesday (2245 GMT Monday).
